claims.text: R0491's registered profile keywords include plain language, health literacy, readability assessment, patient information materials, cognitive accessibility, genetic risk perception and mental models, which are the content-structuring competencies the company says it lacks.
limitations: Profile keywords are self-described research interests, not verified output or deliverable quality.
No evidence in this Run covers pharmacogenomic (CYP2C19/CYP2D6) result content specifically.

claims.text: A randomised experiment by R0491 on patients recently discharged from an internal medicine ward in Vojvodina found that plain-language rewritten discharge summaries substantially improved immediate free recall (M = 7.4 vs 4.1; Cohen's d = 0.89) relative to standard institutional text, but found no significant difference in medication adherence intent at two-week follow-up.
limitations: Single regional hospital sample; recall outcome, not app-specific comprehension.
Authorship shown only by the registered author field excerpt; co-author identities not assessed here.
The adherence null result means readability alone did not change behavioural intent — relevant to the company's 'what it means for my medicine' goal.

claims.text: R0491's participatory evaluation of a hypertension self-management mobile app with 30 low-health-literacy adults found trend-graph interpretation was the most problematic feature (73% of low-literacy participants misread directionality on inverted axes) and that medication reminders averaging 24 words produced substantially higher error rates than reminders of 10 words or fewer; a revised prototype tested with 18 participants showed a 44% reduction in task-error rate.
limitations: Sample was hypertension patients with low literacy in one clinic; not a pharmacogenomic context and not a Serbian/English bilingual setting.
Pre/post comparison between two rounds is not described as randomised or controlled in the excerpt.

claims.text: R0491 authored work on interpreting probability expressions in Serbian screening leaflets: 68% of 32 think-aloud participants from a Novi Sad general-population sample misread positive predictive value as diagnostic certainty, 41% expressed intention to avoid further screening after misunderstanding a false-positive rate, and frequency formats ('3 out of every 100') produced significantly fewer errors than percentages.
limitations: Cervical screening context, not drug-metabolism results; findings may not transfer directly to CYP2C19/CYP2D6 interpretation.
Small qualitative-plus-quantitative sample (n = 32) in a single city.

claims.text: R0491 adapted a Flesch–Kincaid-style index for Serbian (the Serbian Readability Index, SRI) using a corpus of 180 patient information leaflets from Vojvodina pharmacies and clinics, validated with 96 participants via a cloze procedure (R² = 0.74), and the SRI was later used as the readability manipulation check in the plain-language discharge-summary experiment.
limitations: Readability formulas measure text complexity, not comprehension or decision correctness.
Corpus collected 2008–2010; contemporary Serbian digital health language may differ.
SRI is a text-scoring instrument, not a validated app-usability test.

claims.text: R0491's industry-facing track record includes consulting for two pharmaceutical companies on revising Serbian-language patient information leaflets to plain-language standards, external expert review for a health technology company's patient-reported outcomes platform, and co-evaluation of a multi-rater plain-language standard with pharmacists, medical writers, patient representatives and psychologists (ICC(2,1) = 0.81).
limitations: Industry experience is described in a profile field without named clients, deliverables or outcomes.
The plain-language standard evaluation concerned medicines documentation (SmPC-like documents), not pharmacogenomic laboratory reports.

claims.text: R0491's stated collaboration preferences favour joint research on patient-facing digital tools, contract research on assessing and revising health information materials, consulting on readability evaluation methodology, and student internships involving corpus analysis or user testing; she is described as cautious about partnerships that would restrict open publication, and her eye-tracking equipment is available by arrangement.
limitations: Preferences are a profile declaration, not a commitment or availability confirmation.
Eye-tracking access depends on separate arrangement and is unverified; no schedule, cost or capacity is given.

claims.text: Bounded pilot: one working cycle in which R0491 (a) redesigns the patient-facing result explanation into a short structured plain-Serbian/plain-English template anchored on the single question 'does this affect a medicine I currently take', applying frequency-format and short-notification rules from her prior work, and (b) defines a pre-release comprehension test protocol with explicit task-level pass criteria rather than satisfaction ratings.
limitations: Proposed design; no evidence that this template has been tested with pharmacogenomic results.
Clinical accuracy of content remains the company's responsibility; R0491 would not be validating allele interpretation.

claims.text: Validation should combine a readability pre-screen (Serbian Readability Index) with a small think-aloud usability round and a teach-back/own-words outcome similar to the company's 14/20 baseline, plus a short follow-up check on whether patients can name the affected medicine — mirroring the finding that readability gains did not shift adherence intent.
limitations: Company's autumn user test (20 patients, 14/20, Novi Sad pharmacy) is self-reported in the challenge and not independently registered evidence, so it can only serve as a comparator.
Sample sizes required for a defensible claim are unknown and would depend on the effect size actually targeted.

claims.text: Unresolved questions: whether R0491 has Serbian/English bilingual material experience beyond Serbian-focused work (titles and keywords indicate Serbian-language orientation, with one abstract mentioning Serbian and English wording), what publication/open-access terms the company would accept, what ethics approval and data-protection route covers patient testing of real results, and how the app handles probabilistic/metaboliser-status phrasing without implying certainty.
limitations: No evidence in this Run documents R0491's direct experience with pharmacogenomic reports, medical-device/software regulation, or bilingual (Serbian+English) patient material design.
Publication-restriction terms, IP ownership, budget and timeline are not established by any registered Evidence.

summary.text: R0491 (health psychology / health communication, University of Novi Sad) is a strong match for the company's stated gap: structuring plain-language patient information and testing whether it works. Her registered work covers plain-language rewriting of clinical text with measured comprehension effects, participatory evaluation of a mobile health app with low-literacy users, lay misinterpretation of probability statements in Serbian, a Serbian readability index, and multi-rater plain-language standard evaluation.

Fit is strongest on method and content design; there is no registered evidence of pharmacogenomic-report or drug-metabolism content experience, and the earlier finding that readability gains did not shift adherence intent is a material caution for the company's ambition.

technicalRationale.text: Concrete transferable know-how: plain-language rewriting improved immediate recall substantially (d ≈ 0.89) in a Vojvodina patient sample, while adherence intent did not change, so the app should be designed to support the decision, not just reading ease.

Mobile-specific evidence: simplified wording (≤10-word reminders) and simplified visuals reduced task errors, with inverted-axis trend graphs a known failure mode — directly applicable to a phone-sized result screen.
Risk-communication evidence: frequency formats outperformed percentages for lay readers of Serbian screening leaflets, relevant to how metaboliser status and dosing flags are phrased.

Measurement toolkit: the Serbian Readability Index gives an objective pre-screen for the Serbian version; the multi-rater checklist approach (ICC 0.81) offers a template for structured expert review of draft copy.

cooperationScope.text: Proposed first cycle: redesign the patient-facing result explanation into a short question-answer template ('does this affect a medicine I take now?') and deliver a written pre-release test protocol with pass criteria, within the company's stated capacity (designer plus in-house clinical writers).

Modalities consistent with her declared preferences: contract research on assessing and revising health information materials, consulting on readability evaluation methodology, possibly a student internship for corpus/user-testing work.

validation.text: Pre-screen Serbian and English draft copy with the Serbian Readability Index, then run a think-aloud usability round on the short-code flow and a teach-back outcome measured in the patients' own words.
Add a behavioural-intent probe (can the patient state which current medicine is affected and what to do next) because readability alone did not move adherence intent in prior work.
Use structured multi-rater review of draft text with a defined adherence checklist and report inter-rater reliability, rather than single-reviewer sign-off.
Compare pilot results against the company's own 14/20 baseline, treating that baseline as company-reported rather than verified evidence.

constraints.text: Open-publication caution: she is described as reluctant to accept partnerships that restrict publishing results; the company should expect a publication and data-use clause.
Her prior studies were Serbian-language and single-region (Vojvodina/Novi Sad) samples; bilingual Serbian/English product equivalence is unproven.

She would not supply clinical interpretation of alleles; clinical content and pharmacogenomic correctness stay with the company's clinical pharmacists, and she is not evidenced as a regulatory/medical-device expert.

unknowns.text: Confirm her actual availability, contractual terms, and appetite for a small-company engagement; the profile only records stated openness.
Establish whether ethics approval and a data-processing basis exist for testing with real patient results, and whether eye-tracking access is practical and at what cost.
Determine the target effect size and sample size for the pre-release test, and whether the company's self-reported 14/20 baseline is reproducible.
